title: OpenAI and Anthropic use AI to tackle 4D Yang–Mills proof in 1,147-page bid
summary: OpenAI and Anthropic use AI to tackle 4D Yang-Mills proof in 1,147-page bid
detailed: Teams from OpenAI and Anthropic have separately claimed progress on solving the existence problem of four-dimensional Yang-Mills theory using AI.
Both teams built upon a complex mathematical approach pioneered in the 1980s by Tadashi Balaban to handle calculations requiring massive computation.

OpenAI assembled a review committee led by Nobel laureate David Gross to review a formalized version of its proof written in Lean, while the Sussman-Alpöge Anthropic team published its workflow on GitHub.
While verified proof would offer new physics insights, it will not immediately change ongoing particle research because Yang-Mills already successfully explains existing collider data.
sentences: The Yang–Mills theory, which describes forces acting between particles, is widely used in physics but its mathematical foundation has not been completely proved.
A claim that artificial intelligence (AI) has partially filled this gap has been made, and the academic community is now working to verify it.

According to a report in the international journal Science on the 11th (local time), a separate team including researchers from OpenAI and Anthropic each claim to have made progress on the “existence problem of four-dimensional Yang–Mills theory” using AI.
The problem is to prove that this theory is mathematically consistent—free of contradictions—in spacetime composed of three spatial dimensions and one time dimension.
Proposed in 1954 by physicists Chen-Ning Yang and Robert Mills, Yang–Mills theory forms the core of the Standard Model of particle physics.

It provides the framework for explaining the “strong force” that binds the fundamental particles called “quarks” into protons and neutrons inside atomic nuclei, as well as the “weak force” involved in certain radioactive decays.
Calculations based on Yang–Mills theory describe the results of various physics experiments very well.
However, mathematical issues arise in the course of these calculations, such as quantities blowing up to infinity.
Physicists have developed ways to obtain predictions that can be compared with experiments, but they have not rigorously proved that there is an underlying theory that is mathematically consistent.
The two research teams turned to AI to tackle the problem.
One team is from OpenAI; the other is led by Ethan W.
Sussman, a postdoctoral researcher at Northwestern University in the United States, and Levent Alpöge, a researcher at Anthropic.
Both teams drew on an approach pioneered in the 1980s by Tadashi Balaban, professor emeritus of mathematics at Rutgers University in the United States.
This approach requires calculations so complex that they are extremely difficult for humans to carry out.

Antti Kupiainen, a professor at the University of Helsinki in Finland, explained that “Professor Balaban himself acknowledged that there remained additional complicated calculations to be carried out in his approach.” The two research teams brought AI into this kind of work, which demands massive computations and intricate arguments.
“If there is a strategy that looks solvable but the workload is the bottleneck, it is worth handing it over to AI,” Sussman said.
Last month, Sussman and Alpöge unveiled their Yang–Mills results obtained with the help of AI.
Even if the proof is confirmed to be correct, it does not mean that the entire Millennium Prize Problem of “Yang–Mills theory and the mass gap” has been solved.
What the two teams claim to have advanced is the existence problem of the theory.

Instead of publicly releasing the full 1,147-page proof, OpenAI has assembled a committee led by David Gross, a Nobel laureate in physics in 2004 and a professor at the University of California, to carry out the review.
On the 10th, the committee announced the results of its review of a formalized version of the proof written in Lean, a computer language used to check mathematical proofs.
However, this alone is not enough to definitively conclude that the original, as-yet-unreleased proof is correct.
There has also been criticism of the decision not to disclose the full proof.
The Sussman–Alpöge team has made its workflow public on GitHub and is preparing a human-readable paper that others can scrutinize.

“I want to invite everyone to collaborate,” Sussman said, expressing his intention to work with other researchers to produce an explanation that they can understand and build on for follow-up studies.
Even if the latest claims are verified, they are not expected to immediately bring major changes to ongoing research in physics.
That is because Yang–Mills theory already successfully explains the behavior of particles observed at facilities such as the Large Hadron Collider (LHC).

Nevertheless, a rigorous mathematical proof could offer new clues for understanding remaining puzzles, such as how most of the mass of protons and neutrons arises, and why quarks are never observed in isolation.

David Tong, a professor at the University of Cambridge in the United Kingdom, said, “There may be something we’re missing.”
